title: Is there a bank around here?
goal: Ask whether a place exists, say where it is, and tell *ser* from *estar*.

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Perdona, ¿hay un banco por aquí?
dialogs.intro: Asking someone in the street. Watch how *hay* and *está* take turns — that is the whole lesson of this unit.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, is there a bank around here?
lines.literal: forgive, there-is a bank through here?

lines.speaker: Señora:
lines.text: Sí, hay uno en la calle Mayor.
lines.id: Yes, there's one on Mayor Street.
lines.literal: yes, there-is one on street Mayor.

lines.speaker: Señora:
lines.text: No, está cerca. Está al lado de la farmacia.
lines.id: No, it's close. It's next to the pharmacy.
lines.literal: no, it-is-located near. it-is-located at-the side of the pharmacy.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How many minutes away is it?

lines.speaker: Señora:
lines.text: A cinco minutos a pie. Todo recto y a la izquierda.
lines.id: Five minutes on foot. Straight ahead and then left.
lines.literal: at five minutes on foot. all straight and to the left.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And the market? It's closed today, isn't it?
lines.literal: and the market? today it-is-located closed, truth?

lines.speaker: Señora:
lines.text: No, está abierto hasta las dos.
lines.literal: no, it-is-located open until the two.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: ¿Y hay un cajero automático en el banco?

lines.text: Sí, hay dos. Están en la entrada.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Muchas gracias. Usted es muy amable.

notes: **Hay = there is / there are, and it never changes form.** One thing or a hundred, it's still *hay*: *hay un banco*, *hay tres bancos*. It introduces something not yet mentioned — which is why it pairs with *un / una / dos*, never with *el / la*.

**Once the thing is known, estar takes over.** Compare: *Hay un banco en la calle Mayor* (saying it exists), then *El banco está al lado de la farmacia* (saying where it is). This order is almost always right: *hay* first, *estar* after.

**Ser vs estar — the heart of Spanish.** *Ser* is for what something basically is: *Marta es española*, *el mercado es grande*. *Estar* is for where it is and how it is right now: *Marta está en casa*, *el mercado está cerrado*. The wrong choice changes the meaning, not just the sound: *es aburrido* = he's a boring person; *está aburrido* = he's bored.
**Por aquí** = "around here", looser than *aquí*, which means right on this spot. *Por* with a place word always means "around": *por Madrid*, *por el centro*.
**Uno replaces a noun already mentioned.** *Hay uno en la calle Mayor* — *uno* here means "one bank", with no need to repeat *banco*. For feminine nouns: *una*.
**Distance is measured in time.** *Está a cinco minutos* (five minutes away), *a diez minutos en coche*, *a dos horas de Madrid*. Note the *a* — it can't be dropped.
**Usted = formal "you".** Its verb forms are exactly the same as "he/she": *usted es*, *usted tiene*, *usted vive*. In Spain *usted* is used sparingly; in Latin America far more often.
**¿verdad? and ¿no?** Tacked onto the end of a sentence to ask for agreement, just like "right?" or "isn't it?" in English: *Está abierto, ¿verdad?*
**¡Que tenga un buen día!** is a short, very common well-wish. It's actually a subjunctive form — B1 grammar — so just learn it whole. The informal version is *¡que tengas un buen día!*

grammars.title: The verb estar (to be located)
body: *Estar* answers two questions: **where** something is and **how** it is at the moment.
after: Its partner, *ser*, you've been using since Unit 1 — but only its first three forms. Here's the full set: **yo soy, tú eres, él / ella / usted es, nosotros somos, vosotros sois, ellos / ustedes son**. The anchors are the same as for other verbs: the *nosotros* form ends in **-mos**, the *ellos* form in **-n**.

grammars.title: Ser or estar? A decision table
body: When in doubt, ask yourself: **could what I'm saying change tomorrow?** If so, it's almost certainly *estar*.
after: Some adjectives change meaning depending on the verb. The most common: *ser listo* (clever) vs *estar listo* (ready); *ser aburrido* (boring) vs *estar aburrido* (bored); *ser bueno* (good) vs *estar bueno* (tasty, of food); *ser rico* (rich) vs *estar rico* (delicious).

One exception that trips people up: **events** take *ser*, even when you're asking where. *La fiesta es en mi casa* — the party is at my house. But *mi casa está en Bandung*. Things take *estar*, events take *ser*.
